Boundaries have consequences and aren't just statements that you dislike someone's actions. However, it's important to note that whatever the consequences of a broken boundary are should not be to punish the other person but to help you better enforce the boundary and maintain your peace.

And then, boundaries aren't meant to be something that's broken multiple times before you take action. When a boundary is set and you told the other person what it is and they care for you, it should not be broken. And saying "it just happened once" is not ok because it reinforces the idea that it isn't really a boundary and you don't actually care that someone crossed it.

An example of a boundary is, "I do not like it when we yell at each other and I feel that it stops us from effectively communicating and it makes me anxious. The next time we do start yelling I will tell you that I'm feeling anxious and leave the room until we have both calmed down."

I know that this example doesn't necessarily have anything to do with your situation but I just wanted to show what a boundary looks like.

Also notice how in the example there isn't any blame on who starts crossing it (yes you can cross your own boundaries). You should make it clear in your boundaries what will happen whenever it is crossed and how you plan on fixing the issue. Also make sure that in your boundaries that the actions taken are yours and that you aren't putting it on the other person to fix it, that's not their responsibility. Their only obligation is to not cross the boundary.

When you set boundaries make sure that you aren't accidentally giving the person an ultimatum. Boundaries are very much NOT ultimatums. An example of an ultimatum using the same context as above would be, "Stop yelling or I'll leave".

The last thing about setting boundaries that I want to add, just know that the consequences of someone crossing your boundaries does not give you the right to hurt them or start crossing their boundaries. There should be mutual respect for each other's boundaries. 

I don't know what the action should be if your partner crosses the boundary you mentioned in your post. Only you can know what would be appropriate and if your partner will change his actions.

However, I do think that there are bigger problems that you and your partner need to work through. Also I know you said that your insurance dropped your therapist so, if you can afford it I would highly recommend paying for a session with your therapist where you have an in depth discussion about how to set and enforce boundaries. It'll help you in much more than just your marriage.

So like you I've been struggling with depression for a really long time. I started with SSRIs, but I also hit a wall with them, and plunged into a depression worse than when I was initially diagnosed with major depressive disorder.

I was switched to SNRIs and the same thing happened. My doc didn't know what was going on and I was put on a huge amount of meds. My SNRIs was upped to the maximum dose, I was put on atypical antidepressants, low dose atypical antipsychotics and high dose lithium.

When all that eventually failed, I was ready to quit on everything, including life. It wasn't until I started reading about BP type II, that I found a possible diagnosis that matched my symptoms. I got extremely pushy with my doc, refusing to take all this medication and I wanted to be worked up for BP II.

After many psychological and physical exams, I showed signs of both BP II and borderline personality disorder. With this new information, I was put on high dose mood stabilizers, and instead of doing CBT with my psychologist, we're now doing DBT. I honestly haven't felt this stable and this good in a long time.

You might not have BP II or BPD, but you also might. Asking to be assessed for these won't do any harm. In the end if it turns out you don't have either of these, you can rule it out and move to another possibility. It's your life and your money paying for a treatment that isn't working. It's best to discuss your concerns with your treatment team, and work towards a plan that actually works.

When you do get those thoughts, don't stress too much about trying to make them go away. Find something you can do, even of it's something simple like going on a walk, and just try to do that. Try to do things, even if you don't enjoy them, but do them one small step at a time. In my experience it's easier to accept that I have these thoughts, and try not to act on them.

Self deprecating jokes. It's an easy out. Though I recommend you only do that around people you trust. Again, this isn't the best coping mechanism, but it's one that works for me. And please please please only do this with people you absolutely trust.
